title: SLO Prognostics and Capacity Quarantine Playbook
author: Nora Chen
content:
Overview
--------
This playbook defines a combined approach for (1) predictive SLO prognostics using telemetry signals, (2) automated and manual capacity quarantine actions to protect defined business-critical SLOs, and (3) the incident review / remediation cadence that follows quarantine activations. It is intended for platform SREs, service owners, and product stakeholders responsible for multi-tenant inference and serving runtime availability.

Goals
- Detect SLO drift early using leading indicators (not just rolling error budgets).
- Contain and stabilize critical SLOs by isolating tenant/capacity shock via a "capacity quarantine" process.
- Provide a clear operational runbook and post-incident evidence checklist for reviews and capacity corrections.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood inference-serving services (hosted and dedicated control planes) and multi-tenant GPU pools.
- Targets SLOs with business impact: 99th tail latency, request availability, and embedding-return correctness windows.
- Does NOT replace tenant eviction / billing enforcement policies; quarantine is a temporary stabilization mechanism.

Key Definitions
- Prognostic signal: A telemetry-derived metric that historically precedes SLO burn (examples: model KV cache miss rate spike, median GPU utilization delta, inter-request latency jitter).
- Capacity quarantine: Engineering action that restricts incoming traffic to a subset of tenants or routes, reassigns requests to slower fallbacks, or pins model variants to preserve critical SLOs.
- Critical SLOs: SLOs categorized as P0/P1 by product impact (see SLO attribute table).

Ownership and Roles
- SRE on-call: Execute quarantine runbook and initial containment; page service owner.
- Service owner (team owning model or API): Validate quarantine target tenants, approve broad mitigations, drive postmortem.
- Capacity engineering: Execute capacity scale-up/soft-preemption and advise on reserve capacity usage.
- Observability engineering: Maintain prognostic signals and dashboards; run simulation backtests quarterly.

SLO Attribute Matrix (example)
| SLO name | Objective | Primary metric | Burn threshold (30m) | Critical? | Notification channel |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| request-availability | 99.95% | successful_requests/total_requests | >0.1% error | YES | #sre-pager, slack SRE-alerts |
| p99-latency | 1000ms | 99th latency (ms) | >1.5x baseline | YES | #sre-pager |
| embedding-cost-trim | 98% | normalized embedding completeness | >2% regression | NO | #platform-observability |

Leading Prognostic Signals (examples and rationale)
- KV cache miss rate (per-model): sustained +15ppts in 10m often precedes p99 latency burn when model cache reuse is high.
- GPU scheduling preemption count: sudden uptick correlates with cross-tenant eviction and tail latency increases.
- Request inter-arrival jitter: high jitter signals bursty traffic that will drive queue growth.
- Prefix-caching hit-rate and token re-generation ratio: poor values often indicate prompt churn and increased compute per request.

Telemetry thresholds and alert types
- Signal-critical alert (page): any single prognostic signal breaching its page threshold (table below) for 5 minutes.
- Signal-warning alert (ops): sustained breach for 10 minutes or two signals correlated across traces.

Example alert thresholds (tune per service)
| signal | warning | critical | purpose |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| model_kv_cache_miss_rate (5m) | >8% | >15% | early cache evaporation indicator |
| gpu_preempt_count (5m) | >2 | >5 | capacity stranding / noisy neighbor |
| req_interarrival_p95_delta | >200ms | >500ms | burstiness that drives queues |

Capacity Prognostics and Quarantine Decision Matrix
1. Detect: Observability pipeline correlates prognostic signals with SLO burn probability > 60% in next 30m (see prognostics model scoring below).
2. Validate: On-call inspects recent traces, model hotness, and tenant distribution.
3. Contain (automated/fast): If predicted impact > 75% and critical SLOs are at risk, trigger automated partial quarantine: route 20–50% of non-critical tenant traffic to slow-path fallback, enable tighter concurrency caps, and raise preemption buffers.
4. Escalate (manual/stopgap): If automated containment insufficient, on-call initiates full capacity quarantine for specified tenants/routes.

Quarantine action catalog (examples)
- Route-level throttles: apply token-bucket rate limits to defined API routes for non-critical tenants.
- Tenant soft-throttle: reduce max concurrent requests per tenant by 30–70%; prefer queueing over outright rejection.
- Model fallback routing: switch heavy requests to quantized or smaller model variants with known latency characteristics.
- Reserve capacity allocation: allocate reserved headroom (if available) to critical routes and pin their worker pools.

Runbook: Capacity Quarantine Activation (step-by-step)
1. On-call receives signal-critical page or prognostic dashboard indicates >75% impact probability.
2. Triage (5 minutes): confirm signal provenance (edge, load balancer, serving runtime), check recent deploys, and confirm there is no active global outage.
3. Notify stakeholders: post initial incident summary in Slack SRE-alerts and tag service owner + product owner.
4. Execute automated partial quarantine policy (runbook script):
   a. Run: ./ops/quarantine/trigger_partial.sh --service SERVICE --policy cache-stabilize-20
   b. Monitor telemetry for 2 minutes. If no improvement, proceed.
5. If continued deterioration (15 minutes): coordinate with service owner to identify hot tenants and run full quarantine.
   a. Use tenant selector: ./ops/quarantine/select_tenants.py --service SERVICE --mode hot-tenants --max 10
   b. Apply: ./ops/quarantine/activate_full.sh --tenant-list TENANTS.csv --reasons "kv_miss_spike,gpu_preempt"
6. Confirm stabilization: SLO metrics trending back toward baseline for 30 minutes.
7. Begin staged de-escalation per Deactivation checklist below.

Deactivation checklist
- Confirm SLOs have recovered (30m stable window).
- Incrementally remove throttles in 10% steps every 5 minutes while observing for regressions.
- Revert model routing if fallbacks are no longer required.
- Re-run traffic replay for any quarantined tenants in a test environment to validate capacity correction.

Incident review and evidence standards (post-activation)
Required artifacts for any quarantine activation:
- Timeline: exact timestamps for prognostic alerts, quarantine triggers, throttle changes, and stakeholder notifications.
- Telemetry export: 1h pre-incident and 2h post-incident raw metrics for signals used in detection.
- Trace samples: 20 representative distributed traces (10 before, 10 after) that show latency and queue behavior.
- Tenant list and request patterns: CSV of quarantined tenant IDs and the request counts during the incident window.
- Runbook actions: exact CLI commands used, approver signatures (Slack thread IDs).

Postmortem minimum required sections
1. Summary and impact (customers, internal).
2. Detection timeline and prognostic signal analysis.
3. Containment actions taken and rationale.
4. Root cause hypothesis and evidence linking capacity signals to SLO regression.
5. Follow-up actions (owner, priority, due date).
6. Capacity corrections: reserve changes, autoscale policy adjustments, model variant scheduling tweaks.

Operational tooling (dashboards, queries, automation)
- Dashboards: prognostic overview (heatmap of per-model KV miss, GPU preemption, tenant QPS skew), quarantine status center, SLO impact forecast.
- Automation scripts: ops/quarantine/* (partial and full activation), ops/prognostics/backtest.py, ops/prognostics/score_model.py.
- Alerting rules (Prometheus-style examples):
  - rule: HighModelKVMiss
    expr: increase(model_kv_cache_miss_total[5m]) / increase(model_req_total[5m]) > 0.15
    for: 5m
    labels: {severity: page}

Prognostics model (brief)
- We maintain a lightweight logistic classifier that consumes the normalized prognostic signals and outputs a probability of SLO burn in the next 30 minutes. The model is retrained weekly on labeled incidents. Observability engineering owns the model and validation harness.
- Backtest every quarter across five representative services and publish ROC/AUC and calibration plots to the prognostics dashboard.

Simulated exercise schedule (reliability initiative)
- Quarterly capacity-quarantine drills: run a game-day where prognostic signals are seeded and teams execute the quarantine runbook. Objectives: validate tenant selection tooling, measure time-to-stabilize, and ensure postmortem artifacts are captured.
- Annual audit: validate that critical SLOs have appropriate reserve capacity and the prognostics model false-positive rate is < 5%.

Metrics to track for playbook health
- Mean time to quarantine activation (target < 12m from page).
- Mean time to stabilization after quarantine (target < 30m).
- Quarantine correctness: % of quarantines that targeted true root-cause tenants (target > 85%).
- Prognostics precision/recall (internal SLA for the prognostics model).

Example queries and snippets (appendix)
- Latency tail trend (Influx/PromQL):
  increase(requests_total{job="service",route="/v1/generate"}[15m])
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- Simple tenant selector (pseudo-CLI):
  ./ops/quarantine/select_tenants.py --service inference-api --metric kv_miss_rate --since 10m --top 5 > TENANTS.csv

Change control and approval for persistent capacity changes
- Any persistent change to reserve capacity, concurrency caps, or default model routing that lasts >24 hours requires a signed Change Request and approval from Capacity Engineering and Product. Log CR in change-management template and link in postmortem.

References and related pages
- See also: SLO admission playbook, capacity-onboarding-runway, prognostics model repo.
